https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/world/868891/.text: Skip to main content 3 August 2026, 6:50am Two die as firefighting helicopters collide in Greece, French blaze changes course From Caption: Firefighters and Hellenic Civil Protection personnel battle advancing flames during a wildfire near Agios Nektarios in Western Attica, Greece. Photo credit: NICK PALEOLOGOS / AFP Dane and Greek national die in one helicopter, others survive Investigation suggests sparks from power network started blaze Major fire in France changes course as wind shifts Danube's low level prompts Hungary to shut nuclear plant Two firefighting helicopters collided in Greece while helping to control a huge wildfire on Sunday that has destroyed more than 100 homes northwest of Athens, while people fled another blaze on the tourist island of Kefalonia. Two people on one helicopter - a Greek and a Danish national - died, while the crew on the other - one person from Greece, one from Britain - survived, the fire service said. Investigations had started into what caused the collision, it added. Europe has been ravaged by wildfires this summer after a period of record-breaking heatwaves and little rain, conditions that scientists say have been exacerbated by climate change. Destructive blazes in France and Spain showed some signs of easing over the weekend, but several wildfires have broken out in Greece after a period of relative calm there. The two helicopters collided in the area of Psatha in the Attica region, Greece's fire service said in a statement. Video posted on the Forecast Weather Greece Facebook page appeared to show two helicopters closing to cross paths at low altitude, before the main rotor of the lower helicopter struck the underside of the other. The lower one then crashed in flames. The second helicopter then dumped its load of water and flew away. Reuters has not verified the authenticity of the footage. Investigations suggested the fire that started in the Greek region of Boeotia before spreading to Attica was caused by sparks from conductors on a private network transmitting electricity generated by wind turbines to the main power grid, the eKathimerini website reported. Two Greek nationals were arrested on suspicion of negligence, while another suspect remains at large, the report said. 'Force of nature' Gale-force winds that had fuelled a fire around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth 60km northwest of Athens subsided, but flames crossed a mountain to the south and reached the settlement of Veniza and a military firing range, igniting unexploded ordnance. Emergency crews focused their efforts on preventing fire from advancing towards the coastal town of Megara, which has a population of around 30,000. "There are moments when the force of nature and the intensity of weather conditions exceed all human planning and every operational capability," Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in his regular Sunday message. Greek authorities issued emergency alerts for evacuations for a number of settlements in western Attica, including an industrial estate near Megara. In the village of Agios Konstantinos, residents were doing their best to halt the spread of the blaze. "The fire has been burning since last night, it is certain that they cannot have forces everywhere. We as residents are doing everything we can," said Tasos Tzempelikos, 61, who along with his son was pouring water on the fire. Overnight, several settlements on the Ionian island of Kefalonia were evacuated after a fire broke out in the Pastra area in the south. Fire in France changes course In France, a fire in the southwestern Var region switched direction after a change in the wind and surged into a forested area that was difficult to access, BFM TV reported. A new fire also broke out alongside a highway near the historic southern city of Carcassonne, apparently caused by a blazing vehicle, BFM TV added. Video on the channel showed huge plumes of billowing grey smoke and flames near the road. Authorities said they had closed the highway and evacuated a nearby animal park. In Montfort-sur-Argens in Var, Georges Blanc, who had fled the fire earlier, returned home and was busy putting out hot embers to prevent a flare-up, while firefighters watered the wider area. "With the combined efforts of the two Canadairs (firefighting planes) and the firefighters, I think you could say all the houses were saved... And now, well, I'm coming back to check, because since I saw the flames, I thought the houses wouldn't have survived," he told Reuters. In central Spain, wildfires that ripped through tens of thousands of hectares over the past week were mostly under control, though firefighters were dealing with reignitions in some areas. In the western province of Caceres, a forest blaze erupted on Saturday, prompting the evacuation of around 800 people. Those residents were allowed to return on Sunday but remained confined to their homes as the fire was still active. Hungary nuclear plant forced to shut Other European countries are struggling with drought and receding water levels in major rivers, including the Rhine and the Danube, which recorded its lowest-ever water levels in Hungary, Serbia and Romania. Hungary faces a critical five days, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, as the drying out of the Danube forced the country's sole nuclear power plant to shut for the first time in more than four decades , with a new heatwave looming. Falls in water levels amid a lack of rain have also disrupted shipping and tourism in Hungary and triggered water-use restrictions in more than 100 cities and villages. Danube levels in Serbia fell to their lowest since 1985, cutting the daily output of the country's biggest hydropower plant to only 20 percent, the energy minister said on Sunday. - Reuters 3 August 2026, 6:50am Related stories Europe wildfires: Greece battles fresh blazes as France, Spain improve France and Spain win some respite, as wildfire battles rage across Europe Hungary's Paks nuclear plant could be powered down as Danube water dries up What are 'fire clouds', the ominous phenomenon seen in France? https://artdaily.com/news/198892/Major-R.text: Home Last Week Artists Architects Galleries Museums Photographers Photography PhotoGallery Games Subscribe Comments Search Contact Major Raimonds Staprāns retrospective to open at Latvian National Museum of Art Raimonds Staprāns. The Rothko Barn. 2007–2010. Oil on canvas. Family collection. Photo: Valdis Ošiņš. RIGA .- Marking the centenary of the outstanding Latvian émigré artist, playwright and painter Raimonds Staprāns, the Latvian National Museum of Art presents the exhibition Raimonds Staprāns. The Architecture of Silence from 14 August 2026 to 17 January 2027 in the museum’s 4th-floor galleries. The centenary exhibition of Raimonds Staprāns (1926–2026) aims to introduce works never seen before in Latvia while providing a focused yet comprehensive overview of the artist’s career – from his earliest paintings of the 1950s to the last ones created in the 21st century. In the spring of 2025, the exhibition curator, Dr. art. Elita Ansone, had the opportunity to select paintings for the exhibition at the Latvian National Museum of Art directly from the artist’s studio in San Francisco. The resulting selection reveals the evolution of Staprāns’ distinctive painterly language over the course of seven decades. Raimonds Staprāns’ artistic development coincided with the flourishing of Abstract Expressionism. Yet despite his attempts to paint abstractly, Staprāns found himself continually drawn to figurative landscapes and still lifes. Remaining faithful to these subjects, he became associated with the Bay Area Figurative movement. From Abstract Expressionism, Staprāns absorbed what he called the “architecture” of painting – the structural principles by which a painting is constructed. “A painting must be able to stand like a building,” the artist remarked. His painting is enigmatic, distinguished by rigorously architectural compositions and a colour palette brought to an extreme intensity, charged with inner tension. This is an intellectual language of painting – Staprāns does not explain the world, but, through precise visual means, creates a space of silence imbued with emotional and aesthetic intensity. Each of his paintings is like a finely cut diamond, shaped through a long and deliberate process. The year 2026 marks the centenary of Raimonds Staprāns, commemorated in Latvia with a number of cultural initiatives and events. In October, director Pēteris Krilovs’ docudrama The Red Barn (Sarkanais šķūnis) is scheduled for release. At the opening of Raimonds Staprāns’ exhibition The Architecture of Silence on 13 August, the artist’s memoir 46 Episodes, With and Without Irony will be launched. Based on Staprāns’ personal recollections, the memoir reaches far beyond the individual experience, becoming an important testimony to its time for future generations. The book is of outstanding cultural and historical significance, encompassing a broad and interconnected range of experiences – from the cultural and political life of interwar Riga to the experience of wartime displacement and the artist’s creative and professional development in exile and in the United States. At the end of the Second World War, Raimonds Staprāns fled to Germany with his family at the age of eighteen. In 1947, the family emigrated to the United States, settling in Salem, Oregon. In 1948, Staprāns began studying painting and drama at the University of Washington in Seattle, earning his Bachelor of Arts degree (1948–1952), and completing his Master of Fine Arts at the University of California, Berkeley (1952–1954). San Francisco later became his home, where Staprāns established himself as both a painter and a playwright. Throughout his life, Raimonds Staprāns remained deeply connected to his homeland. As early as the 1960s, he and his wife, the scientist Ilona Staprāne, travelled clandestinely from Moscow to Latvia. In 1972, the artist sent a selection of paintings for an exhibition in Riga. However, the exhibition was closed by Soviet cultural officials the very next day and made inaccessible to the public. Latvian audiences were finally introduced to Staprāns’ work in 2006, when the Latvian National Museum of Art presented the most comprehensive exhibition of his oeuvre ever held in his native country. Over the course of his career, Raimonds Staprāns held more than 60 solo exhibitions. Author’s works are represented in the collections of the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Oakland Museum of California, Los Angeles County Museum of Art, San José Museum of Art, Portland Art Museum, Pasadena Museum of Art, Phoenix Art Museum, Crocker Art Museum, Santa Barbara Museum of Art, Museum of Fine Arts in Houston, the John F. Kennedy Museum of Art (USA), and the Latvian National Museum of Art. The exhibition Raimonds Staprāns. The Architecture of Silence is implemented by the Latvian National Museum of Art in collaboration with the Andrejs Žagars Cultural Development Foundation in partnership with the Riga City Council and https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: The UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, is shown a drone used by French police trained in stopping migrants boarding small boats, at Zuydcoote beach in northern France. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA View image in fullscreen The UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, is shown a drone used by French police trained in stopping migrants boarding small boats, at Zuydcoote beach in northern France. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA Immigration and asylum UK paying £56,000 for each person returned to France under ‘one in one out’ scheme Home secretary defends cost, saying it is about the same or cheaper than putting someone up in a hotel for a year Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Tue 15 Sep 2026 14.34 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 15.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The government’s “one in, one out” deal is costing about £56,000 for every person sent back to France, Shabana Mahmood has told MPs. The home secretary disclosed the figure as she was questioned by the home affairs select committee over whether the scheme was delivering value for taxpayers. About 1,400 people have been removed to France by the Home Office since the scheme began in August 2025, although some have subsequently returned to the UK in lorries or small boats. Asked how much each return had cost, Mahmood said: “I’ll need to write to the committee on the most recent figures. “I think it’s per person for the numbers that have been returned so far, it’s about £56,000.” She later defended the cost, saying it was “still cheaper, or just about the same as supporting someone in a hotel for a year”. Under the deal, the UK sends a person who arrives by small boats back to France in exchange for taking an asylum seeker applying through a legal route. The pilot has already been extended once and is now due to run into October, with its long-term future still to be decided. France wants the bilateral arrangement to be eventually replaced by a wider EU-UK returns deal. An EU-wide returns deal known as the Dublin agreement existed before the UK left the EU. Attempts to continue the returns deal post-Brexit have been rejected by EU leaders. Mahmood dismissed suggestions an EU-wide system would be a “silver bullet” for the Channel crisis. She said the deal had already returned more migrants than Britain ever managed under the EU’s old Dublin arrangements. “It is a real mistake to think that that pact is the future. And if we were in that, this problem would go away because I promise you, it would not,” she said. She said the government’s scheme had struggled to scale up to larger numbers of returns, adding that it had been “operationally difficult” to increase removals because of constraints such as detention space. “It’s not been without its challenges. Obviously, the numbers are still relatively small,” she said. Laurent Nuñez, the French interior minister, has told Mahmood that he wants to end the scheme, it emerged earlier this week. In June, Nuñez told a French parliamentary inquiry: “For our part, we want to move away from this bilateral relationship with the UK. We consider that France should not have to carry it alone, and that it would be better to integrate it into an agreement between the EU and UK. “So I have already clearly told my counterpart that this pilot agreement, which we signed in August 2025, was not intended to be renewed beyond October 1, 2026.” Mahmood told the committee only “relatively small numbers” of rejected asylum-seeking families had taken up a separate pilot offering them as much as £40,000 to voluntarily leave Britain. She said: “If you’re a failed asylum-seeking family, what you’re trading off is an offer of £40,000, which will help you resettle back in your country of origin, versus, you know, access to free healthcare and education for your children.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum Migration Shabana Mahmood Refugees European Union France news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘Signs of violence’: asylum seekers arriving in France injured after being deported from UK ‘They’re lifesavers’: the Birmingham clinic giving hope to traumatised asylum seekers Hundreds of asylum seekers removed from UK to France have disappeared, say NGOs Police working to protect RNLI in Dorset amid opposition to small boat rescues British family pleads with French authorities to release body of relative who died in Channel Number of asylum seekers living in hotels across UK halves in a year Forty children reported missing from UK asylum hotels still not found Woman stranded in Spain after UK’s eVisa system mistakes her for twin sister Home Office could be blocked from deporting trafficking victims to Albania Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://nineoclock.ro/indian-prime-minis.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi hails Captain Smit Machchhar for courage that helped avert tragedy Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has praised Flydubai Captain Smit Machchhar for his extraordinary courage and presence of mind after the pilot was seriously injured during an attack by his co-pilot on an Israel-bound flight, saying that his actions demonstrated to the world that Indians are willing to risk their lives to save others. Prime Minister Modi spoke to Captain Machchhar over a video call on Friday, October 2, 2026, while the pilot was recovering from his injuries, and described him as a hero who helped prevent a major tragedy. “You suffered such a serious injury and fought your own battle between life and death. Even at that moment, you did not think about your own life; you thought about the lives of all the passengers,” Prime Minister Modi told the pilot. The conversation took place on Gandhi Jayanti, the national holiday marking the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi. Referring to Gandhi’s philosophy, Modi told Captain Machchhar: “Today is Gandhi Jayanti, you have shown the world what the true meaning of ‘ahimsa’ (non-violence) is.” Captain Machchhar, who described Modi as his “biggest idol”, is recovering from wounds sustained during the mid-air confrontation. He is currently receiving medical treatment in Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk for injuries suffered in the incident. According to the information released following the incident, Captain Machchhar was attacked by his co-pilot during a Flydubai flight travelling to Tel Aviv. The aircraft was carrying 174 passengers, including 27 children. Despite being seriously injured, Captain Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door after realising that the aircraft was losing altitude. Passengers then intervened and overpowered the co-pilot, while two other pilots on board took control of the aircraft. The plane subsequently made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. Investigations into the incident are ongoing. Recalling the critical moments of the confrontation, Captain Machchhar told Prime Minister Modi that his 17 years of flying experience made him immediately understand the potential consequences for the passengers if he failed to act. “I was lying on the floor of the cockpit injured. I was still getting hit, but realised that the plane was losing altitude. I told myself to give it one last try and open the door,” Machchhar said. He explained that, although he was fighting for his own survival, he could not bear to think about what might happen to the passengers if he did not act. “With whatever energy was left in me, I managed to act and open the door,” the pilot said, adding that the passengers subsequently intervened and helped prevent a catastrophe. Captain Machchhar also told Modi that he regularly recites the Hanuman Chalisa when he faces difficult situations and that he did so during the incident. Prime Minister Modi praised the pilot’s bravery, presence of mind and composure, saying that Captain Machchhar had made a critical decision within a fraction of a second and helped save the lives of many people. “After this incident, the country can proudly say that Indians are not those who take lives, but those who are willing to risk their lives to save others, ” Modi said. The Indian Prime Minister also stressed the broader significance of Machchhar’s actions, saying that had the pilot not acted, questions could have been raised about Indians, Indian pilots and the country’s aviation safety record. “You have truly done a great thing,” Modi told him. In a message following the incident, Prime Minister Modi had earlier described Captain Machchhar as an example of the “highest form of courage”, saying that the pilot had acted without fearing for his own life. “140 crore Indians salute Captain Smit and are praying for his well-being,” Modi said, referring to India’s population. During the video call, Modi again praised the pilot for putting the safety of the passengers ahead of his own. “At that time, you received so many injuries and were engaged in a fight of life and death. But you ignored your own safety and were concerned about the safety of the passengers. You have enhanced the honour of 140 crore Indians. I feel proud from the bottom of my heart,” the Prime Minister said. Captain Smit Machchhar’s actions have attracted widespread attention in India and abroad, with the pilot being praised for his courage and determination in a situation that placed the lives of everyone on board at risk. As investigations continue into the circumstances surrounding the cockpit attack, Captain Machchhar remains under medical care, while Prime Minister Modi and millions of Indians have expressed their support and wishes for his recovery.
